title: Limits and Continuity — Resources and Reference
topicTitle: Limits and Continuity — Resources and Reference
notes: Exercise 15.1 — Foundations of Limits
Key topics covered: Review of equations of straight lines, function definition, value of function, and introduction to limits.
Essential prerequisite: Understanding of domain, range, and composition of functions before approaching limits.
Exercise 15.2 — Trigonometric Limits
Standard trigonometric limits:

• $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$
  • $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x}{x} = 1$
  • $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x} = 0$
  • $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin ax}{\sin bx} = \frac{a}{b}$
  • $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan ax}{\tan bx} = \frac{a}{b}$
  • $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin ax}{\tan bx} = \frac{a}{b}$
Exercise 15.3 — Continuity and Differentiability
Right-hand limit, left-hand limit, continuity of functions, and discontinuities.
Continuity at a point: $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
Left and right continuity: $f$ is left-continuous at $a$ if $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = f(a)$; right-continuous if $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$.
Key Reference Tables
Standard limits at zero: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1+x)}{x} = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a^x - 1}{x} = \ln a$.
Standard limits at infinity: $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 0$, $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\cos x}{x} = 0$, $\lim_{x \to \infty} (1 + \frac{1}{x})^x = e$.
Limits of polynomials: For any polynomial $P(x)$, $\lim_{x \to a} P(x) = P(a)$.
Limits of rational functions: For rational $R(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$, $\lim_{x \to a} R(x) = R(a)$ provided $Q(a) \neq 0$.
Important Theorems
Squeeze Theorem: If $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ near $a$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.
Intermediate Value Theorem: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $k$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, there exists $c \in (a, b)$ with $f(c) = k$.
Sum/Difference rule: $\lim[f(x) \pm g(x)] = \lim f(x) \pm \lim g(x)$.
Product rule: $\lim[f(x) \cdot g(x)] = \lim f(x) \cdot \lim g(x)$.
Quotient rule: $\lim[f(x)/g(x)] = \lim f(x) / \lim g(x)$ (provided denominator limit $\neq 0$).
Constant multiple rule: $\lim[c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot \lim f(x)$.
confusion: A limit describes the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ APPROACHES $a$, not the value of $f(a)$. The limit can exist even if $f(a)$ is undefined.
The Squeeze Theorem requires the squeezing functions to approach the SAME limit from both sides — check both bounds carefully.
Continuity at a point requires three conditions simultaneously: $f(a)$ must exist, the limit must exist, and they must be equal. Missing any one condition means discontinuity.
The IVT guarantees existence but NOT uniqueness — there may be multiple values of $c$ satisfying $f(c) = k$.
practice: Use the Squeeze Theorem to show that $\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin(1/x) = 0$.
Show that $f(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ can be made continuous at $x=2$ by defining $f(2) = 4$.
Prove that $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$ has a root between $x = -1$ and $x = 3$ using the IVT.
universalFacts: Limits are the foundation of all calculus — derivatives and integrals are defined as limits.
The concept of limit was rigorously formalized by Cauchy and Weierstrass in the 19th century using the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition.
A function can have a limit at a point where it is not defined (removable discontinuity).
Limits exist if and only if the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit.
The number $e \approx 2.71828$ arises naturally as $\lim_{n \to \infty} (1+1/n)^n$ and is fundamental to calculus.
